statements.text: Destroying an unwilling person’s only home is a rights-violating use that is presumptively impermissible.
Depriving someone of their sole livelihood without consent is presumptively impermissible, though less severe than rendering them homeless.
Providing life-preserving aid to many people creates a duty of rescue when it can be done without violating stronger negative duties.
Plan A is impermissible because it violates Mira’s stronger right not to be rendered homeless.
Plan C is presumptively impermissible because it violates Sal’s right to livelihood, unless no other plan can substantially relieve comparable or greater risks without such violation.
Plan B avoids rights violations while providing some rescue benefit, so it is permissible.
Between Plans B and C, the duty not to wrongfully deprive Sal of livelihood outweighs the extra aid to Jo when another plan supplies significant rescue without rights violations.

raw_response.conclusion: Plan B is provisionally preferable because it secures a significant rescue (cooling twelve households) without violating any individual’s stronger negative rights. Plan A directly violates Mira’s foundational right to a home; Plan C violates Sal’s income right, which still outweighs the additional individual rescue to Jo when some rescue is already possible without that violation.
raw_response.strongest_objection: Jo endures the greatest heat exposure; Plan C uniquely relieves that extreme risk.
raw_response.answer_to_objection: The council’s stronger duty not to wrongfully strip Sal of his livelihood prevails over the weaker positive duty to relieve Jo once a rescue option (Plan B) exists that respects all comparable rights.
raw_response.reversal_condition: If Jo’s heat exposure rose to an immediate life-threat level while Sal could survive eight weeks without catastrophic loss, the priority between duties might invert, favoring Plan C.
residual_disagreement: Whether uncompensated eight-week closure is less severe than homelessness
Whether positive rescue for extreme heat should override livelihood in emergencies

paper_attribution.title: A Contractualist Argumentation Framework for Moral Decision-Making

evidence.value: During a heat wave, a council has funds for one of three technically feasible cooling plans. Plan A cools twenty households but requires demolishing Mira's occupied home, leaving her without housing; she refuses. Plan B cools twelve of those same households and displaces nobody. Plan C cools Jo's home, which has the greatest heat exposure of any home in this case, but requires closing Sal's only shop for eight weeks without compensation, depriving Sal of income during that period. Sal refuses. Jo's home is not cooled by A or B. Mira, Jo, and Sal are not members of the twenty households. No additional cooling, relocation, or compensation plan is available in this exercise. The text stipulates these effects, not total welfare scores or a ranking of whose overall position is worst. Which plan should the council adopt?
